stories.headline: Kishtwar terror attack case: NIA files chargesheet
stories.title: Kishtwar terror attack case: NIA files chargesheet
stories.summary: Jammu, Oct 9: The National Investigation Agency (NIA) on Friday filed a chargesheet before the NIA Special Court Jammu against an arrested accused and three killed Pakistani terrorists in the Kishtwar terror attack case. In a statement, NIA said it filed the 535-page chargesheet against arrested accused Maneer Ahmed, son of Mohammad Yousuf Koli, resident of Naidgam Chatroo, Inderwal, Kishtwar and three killed terrorists including Saifullah @ Saifullah Kashmiri @ Atiq Nazir @ Atiq Ur Rehman. The chargesheet pertains to the terror attack on 22nd February 2026 at Chatroo, Wani Mohalla, Passer Kote in Kishtwar (RC-03/2026/NIA/JMU). The chargesheet details the conspiracy, the role of the three killed terrorists including Saifullah, a resident of Pakistan and commander of proscribed outfit Jaish-e-Mohammad (JeM), and of arrested accused Maneer Ahmed, along with supporting evidence. It charges Maneer Ahmed with voluntarily harbouring and concealing terrorists involved in attacks on security forces and civilians in hilly district Kishtwar under relevant provisions of UA(P) Act, 1967. NIA has also invoked penal section against the accused terrorists for waging war against India and hatching conspiracy from across the border. As per NIA, the attack involved three terrorists led by terror commander Saifullah, affiliated to Kashmir Tigers (Azrael Group), which acts under the proscribed outfit JeM. Retaliatory fire from security forces led to killing of all three. The group, which was active in upper reaches of Kishtwar, was found to have conducted several attacks that resulted in killing of security forces personnel and locals. Arrested accused Maneer Ahmed has been found to be involved in providing support to the group. NIA’s investigation, spanning almost 5 months, has traced the conspiracy to Pakistan. Further investigation in the case is continuing, the agency in a statement said.

stories.headline: Acharya Vasugupta: The Sage Who Gave Kashmir Shaivism Its First Voice
stories.title: Acharya Vasugupta: The Sage Who Gave Kashmir Shaivism Its First Voice
stories.summary: Every great civilisation has moments when an idea becomes larger than the age in which it is born. In the intellectual history of Kashmir, Acharya Vasugupta represents one such moment. More than a millennium ago, he articulated a vision that became the starting point for one of India’s most sophisticated philosophical traditions—Kashmir Shaivism. Yet Vasugupta’s importance deserves to be understood precisely. He was not the author of the entire philosophical system that later came to be known as Kashmir Shaivism. The elaborate doctrines of the 36 tattvas, Pratyabhijna, Spanda, the various upayas and the aesthetic philosophy associated with Abhinavagupta emerged through generations of thinkers. Vasugupta’s distinctive place lies earlier: he stands at the foundational moment when the central Shaiva insight was expressed as a direct path of recognition and spiritual practice. His name is inseparably associated with the Shiva Sutras, a compact collection of aphorisms that opened a new chapter in Kashmiri thought. In remarkably few words, the text addresses questions that remain fundamental: Who are we? Why do we experience ourselves as limited? What is the relationship between the individual and the universe? And how can that limitation be overcome? The answers were not presented simply as doctrines to be believed. They were framed as invitations to experience. Vasugupta’s precise dates remain uncertain, and the accounts of his life combine history with sacred tradition. He is generally placed around the late eighth or early ninth century CE. Kashmir’s traditional accounts remember him as the sage to whom the Shiva Sutras were revealed. According to one celebrated tradition, Lord Shiva appeared to Vasugupta in a dream and directed him towards a rock on Mount Mahadeva, where the sacred teachings were revealed. Another account holds that the aphorisms were inscribed upon the rock itself and discovered by the sage. Whether understood literally or symbolically, the story expresses the extraordinary status attributed to the text. The Shiva Sutras were regarded not simply as the product of philosophical speculation but as a revelation of a truth that could be directly realised. What Vasugupta Actually Gave the Tradition The most important contribution associated with Vasugupta is the form in which the teaching was transmitted. The Shiva Sutras are not a systematic philosophical treatise. They do not proceed through long arguments or attempt to define every element of a complete metaphysical system. Instead, they offer terse propositions designed to provoke recognition. Their opening declaration is famous: “Chaitanyam Atma” — Consciousness is the Self. The significance of the statement lies not merely in the doctrine it expresses but in the direction it gives to spiritual inquiry. The seeker is asked to begin with the most immediate fact available: the experience of being aware. For Vasugupta, the search for the ultimate does not have to begin somewhere outside the individual. It begins with examining the very nature of the Self. This gives his teaching an important experiential quality. The individual ordinarily identifies the Self with the body, personality, memories, desires and circumstances. Vasugupta’s teaching turns that assumption around. These are changing aspects of experience; the deeper Self is that through which experience is known. The spiritual task is therefore not the acquisition of a new identity but the recognition of an identity that has been obscured by limitation. This is the distinctive seed that later thinkers would develop into the philosophy of Pratyabhijna, or recognition. Vasugupta did not, however, provide the elaborate philosophical formulation later associated with Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta. His contribution was more foundational and direct: he placed recognition at the heart of spiritual practice. That distinction matters. From Revelation to Practice Another distinctive feature of the Shiva Sutras is their practical orientation. The text moves repeatedly from metaphysical insight towards transformation. It deals with meditation, mantra, breath, concentration, perception and states of awareness. Its concern is not simply to explain reality but to show how a seeker might break through the ordinary limitations of experience. This makes Vasugupta different from a philosopher who merely constructs an abstract system. His teaching asks the reader to test the proposition within experience. If the Self is fundamentally free, why do we experience bondage? If the divine is present in all existence, why do we experience separation? If the deepest reality is present here and now, what prevents us from recognising it? These questions are implicit in the structure of the Shiva Sutras. The answer lies in limitation. Human beings habitually identify themselves with a contracted sense of individuality. Kashmir Shaiva thought would later analyse these limitations with considerable technical sophistication, but Vasugupta’s contribution was to establish the spiritual problem in experiential terms. The problem is not that the divine has disappeared. It is that recognition has been obscured. That is a crucial distinction. Liberation therefore becomes less a journey towards a distant goal and more a recovery of what is already present. The Early Vision of Spanda Vasugupta’s name is also closely connected by tradition with the early Spanda teaching. Spanda is frequently translated as “vibration,” although the term should not be confused with a physical vibration. It points towards the subtle dynamism or pulsation of ultimate reality—the fact that the supreme principle is not a lifeless abstraction but possesses the inherent power to manifest, perceive and act. This provided an important bridge between transcendence and the world. If Shiva is ultimate reality and Shakti is the power of manifestation, then creation is not something fundamentally outside the divine. The changing universe is related to the unchanging source through this dynamic power. The Spanda Karikas, traditionally connected with Vasugupta’s lineage, developed this insight. The exact historical relationship between Vasugupta and the text remains a matter of scholarly discussion, and it is therefore safer to speak of the Spanda tradition as belonging to the intellectual circle and lineage associated with him. What matters philosophically is that this early teaching prevented the Kashmir Shaiva vision from becoming a static doctrine of transcendence. Reality is dynamic. The divine is not merely beyond the world; it expresses itself through the world. This would become one of the most fertile ideas in the later development of Kashmir Shaivism. The Foundation and the Edifice After Vasugupta, the tradition expanded dramatically. Somānanda composed the Shivadristi. His disciple Utpaladeva developed the Ishvara Pratyabhijna, giving philosophical precision to the doctrine of recognition. Centuries later, Abhinavagupta brought together multiple streams of Kashmir Shaiva thought and produced a synthesis of extraordinary scope. It is tempting, therefore, to attribute the whole architecture of Kashmir Shaivism to Vasugupta. That would obscure his actual achievement. Vasugupta laid the foundation; the later masters built the philosophical edifice. His achievement was to establish a vocabulary and spiritual orientation from which subsequent generations could work. The Shiva Sutras supplied the compressed foundational insight. The Spanda tradition explored the dynamism of that insight. Later philosophers supplied increasingly elaborate metaphysics, logic and theology. Seen this way, Vasugupta’s importance becomes clearer, not smaller. He was the point at which a powerful spiritual intuition became a transmissible philosophical tradition. Why That Contribution Matters Today This distinction also makes Vasugupta more relevant to the present. The modern world is filled with elaborate systems for describing reality. Science, technology, psychology, economics and artificial intelligence constantly expand our capacity to measure and manipulate the external world. Vasugupta begins somewhere more elementary. He asks us to examine the experiencing subject itself. That question has acquired new urgency. Modern life is increasingly organised around the construction of identity. Professional profiles, social-media personas, biometric data, online reputations and algorithmic recommendations all contribute to the ways in which individuals are represented and understood. Yet none of these representations necessarily answers the simplest question: who is the person behind them? The Shiva Sutras approach this problem from an entirely different direction. Instead of adding another description of the self, they ask us to investigate the basis of selfhood. That is a distinctive contemporary relevance. The second concerns attention. Our age has developed an extraordinary machinery for capturing attention. Notifications, feeds, advertising and recommendation systems continually compete for a person’s mental space. The issue is no longer simply having too much information; it is retaining the ability to determine where one’s attention goes. Vasugupta’s insistence on disciplined awareness therefore acquires a new significance. His teaching can be read as a reminder that attention is not merely an economic commodity; it is an element of freedom. A person who cannot direct attention freely is vulnerable to every external demand. A person who can observe thought without immediately becoming captive to it has begun to recover a degree of inner autonomy. This is not a claim that Vasugupta anticipated the digital age. He could not have. His relevance is that he identified a human problem that technology has intensified without creating: the tendency to lose ourselves in the movements of the mind. There is also a deeper contemporary challenge. Humanity now possesses unprecedented technological power. Artificial intelligence, biotechnology, digital networks and automation are transforming what human beings can do. But increased capability raises a corresponding question: what kind of person should possess that capability? Vasugupta’s philosophy does not provide a technological policy manual. It offers something more fundamental—the insistence that outer power and inner understanding are not the same thing. A civilisation may become increasingly powerful without becoming increasingly wise. That distinction may be one of the most important reasons to revisit India’s philosophical inheritance today. A Beginning, Not a Conclusion Vasugupta’s legacy should therefore not be measured only by the doctrines that later came to bear the name of Kashmir Shaivism. His more distinctive contribution was to establish the first great doorway into that tradition. He took an ultimate philosophical question and turned it into a question of immediate experience. He presented the Self not as an object to be discovered somewhere beyond life, but as the starting point of inquiry. He connected metaphysical insight with spiritual practice. And through the Shiva Sutras, he provided later generations with a remarkably compressed set of teachings from which an entire philosophical world could unfold. Somānanda, Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta would deepen, systematise and expand that world. They would develop its logic, metaphysics, theology, aesthetics and psychology. But the foundational gesture remained Vasugupta’s. More than a thousand years later, its force has not disappeared. At a time when people are surrounded by competing definitions of who they are, when attention has become a commodity and when technological power is advancing faster than reflection about its consequences, Vasugupta’s question is strikingly direct: Before we attempt to master the world, have we understood the one who experiences it? That question takes us back to the opening of the Shiva Sutras and to the sage at the beginning of the Kashmiri tradition. Vasugupta did not provide the final word on Kashmir Shaivism. He did something perhaps more consequential. He opened the first door. (The Author is a columnist, a public intellectual and a noted legal eagle)

stories.headline: What does a delayed US trade deal mean for India?
stories.title: What does a delayed US trade deal mean for India?
stories.summary: A delay in the India-US trade deal adds to the uncertainty that’s already weighing on industry but by itself does not represent a major shock to India’s GDP growth outlook, say economists.“The key issue is not simply the timing of the agreement, but whether the delay results in India facing a materially higher and more persistent tariff disadvantage relative to competing exporters,” says Rajani Sinha, chief economist at CareEdge Ratings.Madan Sabnavis, chief economist at Bank of Baroda, says the lack of a deal is a concern but the impact is hard to quantify.“Impact on exports will be there though not much on GDP as a lot of it is made up by service exports.”Indian goods shipments to the US currently face a 10 percent tariff, plus a most favoured nation (MFN) duty which varies across sectors.The 10 percent levy was imposed on India in July under Section 301 of the Trade Act, where the US cited concerns around forced labour.Also Read: India-US trade talks hit a plateau as FM flags tough road aheadThe rate is far below what Indian goods faced a year ago. Last year, India faced a 25 percent “reciprocal” tariff, which was raised to 50 percent after the US added another 25 percent over purchases of Russian oil.The US and India agreed on a framework for an interim deal on February 6, which cut the rate to 18 percent. Days later, on February 20, the US Supreme Court struck down the tariffs US President Donald Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, calling them unconstitutional.Shipments to the US—India’s largest export market, with a 19.8 percent share of outbound shipments—are growing despite the tariffs.Exports to the US rose 6.2 percent to $42.79 billion in April-August this year, according to commerce ministry data, even as talks on a trade deal dragged on. Total merchandise exports jumped 17.9 percent to $215.91 billion over the same period.Last year, front-loading of exports ahead of tariffs had lifted April-June 2025 shipments to the US by 22 percent. A large part of India’s exports to the US such as pharmaceuticals and smartphones remain exempt from tariffs, limiting the damage.Also Read: Nirmala Sitharaman: Global Economy Needs Resilience Amid UncertaintyBut there are worries.President Donald Trump on September 18 signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which authorises tariffs of up to 100 percent on top buyers of Russian energy, India among them.A materially higher tariff under this legislation would represent a significant change in the trade environment and could have much greater implications for Indian exports, investment and growth, says Sinha.Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has, meanwhile, said that both countries have reached “a plateau [on the trade deal] beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult”. This came after US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said talks were close to conclusion but that a deal was not “imminent”.Ajay Srivastava, founder of think tank Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), says the statements signal that there could be an interim agreement, instead of a fully fleshed out trade deal.But with tariffs now almost uniform across countries—rather than, for instance, 50 percent on India against 20 percent on Vietnam—“we are relatively better off without a deal”, he says.Also Read: Why India's trade policy makes imports cheaper than manufacturingRisks to IndiaAn immediate risk could come through financial markets and investor sentiment, feels CareEdge’s Sinha.Sinha warned that a prolonged delay, especially if India is seen as losing ground to other emerging market exporters, could hit portfolio flows and the rupee, which is already weighed down by high crude prices, foreign outflows and a strong dollar.Foreign portfolio investors have net-sold Rs 2.3 lakh crore in this calendar year so far, according to NSDL data.The rupee closed Thursday at 96.78 per dollar, near its all-time low of 96.96.Export-oriented firms may become more cautious about expanding capacity in India if access to the US market becomes increasingly uncertain, says Sinha.GTRI’s Srivastava says uncertainty already complicates pricing and contracts. “If US buyers want to enter into long-term contracts with some Indian firm, they may be conservative,” he says.Earlier this week, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra said it was “premature” to judge the impact of no deal since it was unclear “which sectors, or to what extent, these tariffs will be applied”, adding that the impact would “obviously” be negative. He also pointed to industry having diversified its exports.“At the same time, we’ve had a number of trade agreements in the past. opening: A delay in the India-US trade deal adds to the uncertainty that’s already weighing on industry but by itself does not represent a major shock to India’s GDP growth outlook, say economists.

“The key issue is not simply the timing of the agreement, but whether the delay results in India facing a materially higher and more persistent tariff disadvantage relative to competing exporters,” says Rajani Sinha, chief economist at CareEdge Ratings.
body: Madan Sabnavis, chief economist at Bank of Baroda, says the lack of a deal is a concern but the impact is hard to quantify.

“Impact on exports will be there though not much on GDP as a lot of it is made up by service exports.” Indian goods shipments to the US currently face a 10 percent tariff, plus a most favoured nation (MFN) duty which varies across sectors.
The 10 percent levy was imposed on India in July under Section 301 of the Trade Act, where the US cited concerns around forced labour.
The rate is far below what Indian goods faced a year ago.
Days later, on February 20, the US Supreme Court struck down the tariffs US President Donald Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, calling them unconstitutional.
A large part of India’s exports to the US such as pharmaceuticals and smartphones remain exempt from tariffs, limiting the damage.
But there are worries.

A materially higher tariff under this legislation would represent a significant change in the trade environment and could have much greater implications for Indian exports, investment and growth, says Sinha.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has, meanwhile, said that both countries have reached “a plateau [on the trade deal] beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult”.
This came after US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said talks were close to conclusion but that a deal was not “imminent”.
Ajay Srivastava, founder of think tank Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), says the statements signal that there could be an interim agreement, instead of a fully fleshed out trade deal.
Risks to India.
An immediate risk could come through financial markets and investor sentiment, feels Care.
Edge’s Sinha.

Sinha warned that a prolonged delay, especially if India is seen as losing ground to other emerging market exporters, could hit portfolio flows and the rupee, which is already weighed down by high crude prices, foreign outflows and a strong dollar.
Foreign portfolio investors have net-sold Rs 2.3 lakh crore in this calendar year so far, according to NSDL data.
The rupee closed Thursday at 96.78 per dollar, near its all-time low of 96.96.
Export-oriented firms may become more cautious about expanding capacity in India if access to the US market becomes increasingly uncertain, says Sinha.
GTRI’s Srivastava says uncertainty already complicates pricing and contracts.
“If US buyers want to enter into long-term contracts with some Indian firm, they may be conservative,” he says.

Earlier this week, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra said it was “premature” to judge the impact of no deal since it was unclear “which sectors, or to what extent, these tariffs will be applied”, adding that the impact would “obviously” be negative.
He also pointed to industry having diversified its exports.
“At the same time, we’ve had a number of trade agreements in the past.

Many of them have been operationalised, others are in the pipeline… So all these things will mitigate the effect in case there is an additional tariff on some sectors,” Malhotra said at the post-monetary policy press conference.
Franziska Ohnsorge, the World Bank Group chief economist for Asia, concurs on the last point, calling India’s recent pacts with the EU, the UK and others “a big deal”.

Sinha of CareEdge feels India has considerable scope to diversify its trade relationships, and the continued resilience of exports demonstrates that the economy is not excessively dependent on a single market.
“Nevertheless, the US remains too important to be replaced quickly.”

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Friday (October 9, 2026) declined to intervene in the Tamil Nadu Assembly Speaker’s decision to close disqualification proceedings against a group of All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) legislators who had supported C. Joseph Vijay’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK)-led government during the trust vote in May.
The court observed that the Speaker’s decision could not be challenged by an “interloper”.

A Bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana dismissed a plea filed by advocate P.V. Selvakumar, while observing that the sanctity of the constitutional mandate under the Tenth Schedule, which contains the anti-defection law, must be preserved.
“We are fully with you that sanctity of constitutional mandate must be preserved.
But we must understand workings of a democratic system,” the Bench said.

Mr. Selvakumar approached the Supreme Court after the Madras High Court rejected his petition challenging the Speaker’s June 9 decision to drop the disqualification proceedings against the AIADMK legislators.
The Speaker had acted on a May 27 letter from the party’s general secretary seeking withdrawal of the proceedings.
The High Court had held that Mr. Selvakumar, being a third party to the dispute, had no locus standi to interfere in the internal affairs of the AIADMK.
Advocate Nina Nariman, appearing for Mr. Selvakumar, argued that once the Speaker had entertained the disqualification petition, the proceedings ought to have been taken to their logical conclusion.
The legislators, she submitted, had defied the party whip by supporting the government in the confidence vote.
The Bench, however, drew a distinction between defection and differences that may arise within a political party in a multi-party democracy.

stories.headline: Govt sanctions Rs 603.34 cr incentive for sugarcane farmers
stories.title: Govt sanctions Rs 603.34 cr incentive for sugarcane farmers
stories.summary: The incentive of Rs 709.50 per tonne will supplement the Centre’s Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP), taking the payment to Rs 4,000 per tonne for sugarcane with a sugar recovery rate of 9.5 per cent.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: The incentive of Rs 709.50 per tonne will supplement the Centre’s Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP), taking the payment to Rs 4,000 per tonne for sugarcane with a sugar recovery rate of 9.5 per cent.

Chennai: Tamil Nadu has sanctioned Rs 603.34 crore as a special incentive for sugarcane farmers who supplied their crop to mills during the 2025-26 crushing season, Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare Minister M.R.K. Panneerselvam said on Thursday.
Around 90,000 farmers are expected to benefit from the measure, approved on the directions of Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay.
Payments will be made directly into beneficiaries’ Aadhaar-linked bank accounts, with transfers scheduled to begin from the upcoming Deepavali festival.
For the 2025-26 season, the Centre fixed the FRP at Rs 3,290.50 per tonne for sugarcane linked to a 9.5 per cent recovery rate.
The State’s additional payment will bridge the gap between that amount and the Rs 4,000 price.
Farmers supplying cane with a recovery rate above 9.5 per cent will receive proportionately higher payments, taking their total earnings per tonne beyond Rs 4,000, according to the government.
The assistance will cover growers who supplied sugarcane to the mills that operated during the season.
The government said it had collected farmers’ details, including the quantity of cane supplied, Aadhaar numbers and bank account information, to facilitate identification and payment.
District-level committees headed by Collectors will recommend eligible beneficiaries.
The Directorate of Sugar will scrutinise the recommendations before the incentive is released.
The decision responds to a long-standing demand from sugarcane growers for higher payments and is intended to safeguard their interests, the government said.
